high_priority_articles.summary: From Russia sanctions to reining in Trump: What a Democratic Congress can (and can't) do for Ukraine  The Kyiv IndependentThe midterms and the world  Financial TimesA drubbing in the midterms will make Trump even more dangerous to the entire world  The IndependentHow US Midterms Could Move Stock Markets, Oil Prices And India's Exports  NDTVThe US Midterms and Trump’s Challenge  orfonline.org
high_priority_articles.full_text:
What the US midterms could mean for Ukraine
U.S. President Donald Trump delivers remarks during a campaign rally at Crossroads Arena in Corinth, Mississippi, U.S. on Oct. 26, 2026. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)
For months, Ukraine has faced mounting pressure from U.S. President Donald Trump, as he seeks to secure political gains ahead of the November midterm elections.
With both chambers of Congress at stake on Nov. 3, the key question is how heavily Republicans will lose — and whether the scale of any setback will be enough to shift Washington's foreign policy.
The vote comes at a low point in U.S.-Ukraine relations.
Trump drew fire from U.S. lawmakers, Kyiv, and European capitals for allowing Russian diesel into the U.S. and easing sanctions on Russia, running counter to the West's long-standing strategy for ending the war in Ukraine.
And while Moscow avoids pressure, Kyiv is pressed to end its strikes against Russian refineries while grappling with disruptions in intelligence support and Patriot air defense shipments.
A Democratic victory might give Ukraine a sympathetic Congress and offer greater scrutiny over Trump's foreign policy pivots. However, experts who spoke with the Kyiv Independent say that the U.S. president would ultimately keep firm control over his country's foreign policy.
read also
Pushing Ukraine aid past Trump
This week, U.S. voters will elect all 435 members of the House of Representatives, where Democrats are widely expected to win a majority for the first time since 2020.
The Democratic Party faces steeper — but not insurmountable — odds in the Senate, where only about one-third of the 100 seats are up for a vote, with a mere seven considered toss-ups.
Even if the Democratic Party ends up with 51 Senate seats needed for a majority, they would still need the Republican Party to overcome a filibuster, a U.S. policy where 60 votes are needed in the Senate to pass crucial legislation.
For Kyiv, that is not the end of the road, however.
U.S. senators have shown they can build a bipartisan majority around support for Ukraine, most recently in August, when they passed the Lindsey Graham Act — spearheaded by the late Republican Senator Lindsey Graham — with 86 votes.
But this bipartisan consensus cannot be taken for granted when it comes to Republican lawmakers challenging Trump.
"In today's highly polarized political environment, most lawmakers hesitate to oppose a president of their own party, even when they disagree with his policy choices," James M. Lindsay, a U.S. foreign policy expert at the Council on Foreign Relations, told the Kyiv Independent.
Should Democrats muster enough support to push through a bill on assistance for Ukraine or tougher sanctions against Russia, Trump wields powerful veto rights.
Only a two-thirds supermajority in both chambers can override it, and that number is something Democrats are unlikely to whip up.
"Congress has a poor track record in overturning presidential vetoes, especially in foreign affairs," Lindsay notes.
Still, a Congressional majority would hold some leverage.
Lawmakers could include measures supporting Ukraine in "must-pass" legislation, such as defense appropriations bills or the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA).
Congress would then "dare Trump to veto it," said Daniel Hamilton, a U.S. foreign policy expert at the Brookings Institution. "He is unlikely to do so, since the overall bill funds the Defense Department."
But even when the bill leaves the desk with a presidential signature, there comes another obstacle — the chance of Trump simply ignoring it afterward.
read also
When the president sidelines Congress
It has happened before.
A sweeping Russia sanctions bill, championed by the late Senator Graham, was passed with great fanfare and signed into law by the president in September.
Yet, Trump has not toughened up on Russia since — quite the opposite.
On Oct. 16, the president issued a broad waiver of Graham's sanctions, days after his Treasury lifted restrictions on Russian diesel purchases.
This was not the first time the administration had sidestepped Congress on Ukraine matters either.
Earlier this year, the Pentagon delayed $400 million in military assistance under the Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative (USAI) for months, even though Congress had already authorized it.
This illustrates the limits of Congress's power: passing a law does not guarantee that the executive will carry it out as lawmakers intended.
Ironically, Congress was quite capable of disrupting the White House's Ukraine course during the Biden administration.
The Republican-led House famously blocked a massive aid bill from late 2023 until 2024, leading to a critical ammunition "hunger" among Ukrainian forces.
But this dynamic would not translate to a clash between Trump and a Democratic-led House. For the Ukraine policy he is pursuing, Trump does not need congressional consent, Lindsay said.
"Some presidential powers, such as when to negotiate, whom to negotiate with, and what to negotiate over, are beyond Congress's power to direct, restrain, or regulate."
It was Trump who — to the chagrin of many pro-Ukraine lawmakers — publicly humiliated President Volodymyr Zelensky in the Oval Office in February 2025 and who pulled Russia out of diplomatic isolation by hosting Russian President Vladimir Putin in Alaska a few months later.
"A Democratic House or Congress may bristle at President Donald Trump's diplomacy with Russia, but it cannot compel him to change it," Lindsay said.
Beyond legislation
A Democratic victory would not upend Trump's policy, but could boost Ukraine's voice on Capitol Hill.
If House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries replaces Mike Johnson as speaker, Republican skeptics could no longer keep pro-Ukraine legislation off the floor, as they did with Biden's aid bill.
Majorities in one or both chambers would also give Democrats leadership of committees and allow them to subpoena executive officials.
According to Hamilton, Democrats may use this power to investigate SpaceX founder Elon Musk, U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, or Trump's peace envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.
Musk is allegedly responsible for the temporary throttling of Starlink services in Ukraine, Hegseth is said to be delaying shipments of Patriot missiles, and the U.S. peace envoys have faced scrutiny for at times pushing peace deals favorable to Moscow.
A House majority would also allow Democrats to impeach executive officials, including, for the third time, Trump. This would not guarantee a conviction and removal — a supermajority of senators is needed for that.
Lawmakers who spoke to the Kyiv Independent see the midterm election as a chance to set the legislative agenda on Ukraine and to scrutinize Trump's policies more closely.
"We will use every legislative and oversight tool available to hold this administration accountable and ensure Ukraine receives the security assistance it needs to defend itself," said Mike Levin, a Democratic representative for California's 49th congressional district.
Backchannel deals with the Kremlin, and any disruptions to intelligence sharing or Ukraine's Starlink terminals would face "rigorous oversight" if Democrats win House committee gavels, he told the Kyiv Independent.
Gregory Meeks, a Democratic representative and ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, pledged to work with lawmakers from both parties to push through legislation to "compel the Trump administration to deliver to Ukraine the security, economic, and intelligence support it needs to defend its people from Putin's brutal and illegal invasion."
In his statement for the Kyiv Independent, Meeks further committed to "fixing" the Graham Act, "including by denying President Trump the ability to unilaterally import Russian energy and undermine U.S. national security interests."
Nevertheless, Ukraine is unlikely to be front and center in Democrats' focus after the midterms.
The party's 100-day post-victory plan focuses on issues most pressing for U.S. voters, such as the cost of living and restraining Trump's war against Iran, which has driven up inflation and fuel prices.
Ukraine is far from the top of the agenda.
And even with his back against the wall in the legislature, the president will still have a bite on the international scene.
"Historically, most presidents in this situation have turned to foreign policy, and so Trump is likely to be even more outrageous in some of his initiatives than before, perhaps including working with Putin and (Chinese President) Xi (Jinping) at the expense of Ukraine and Europe," Hamilton said.
"A Democratic Congress would do what it could to block that; how such battles unfold will depend on the specific issues."
Lindsay also argues that Trump appears unconcerned about how unpopular his foreign policy maneuvers are, be it the Russian diesel deal or the sanctions waiver.
And since he cannot run for another term, he has even less incentive to temper his policy, the expert added.
"Those are not decisions of a president who is following the political winds."

Note from the author:
Hi, this is Martin, the author of this article.
After Russia launched its full-scale invasion, the U.S. has been Ukraine's first and foremost ally. American weapons, intelligence, and sanctions have helped Ukraine hold the line.
This alliance now looks fragile. But Ukraine and the U.S. have shown they can weather political storms because their support has never rested on a single president. It rested on lawmakers, voters, and ordinary people who decided that helping Ukraine mattered.

high_priority_articles.title: India Amends Textile PLI Scheme: New Investment Criteria & Round 4 Incentives - India Briefing
high_priority_articles.summary: India Amends Textile PLI Scheme: New Investment Criteria & Round 4 Incentives  India Briefing
high_priority_articles.full_text:
The central government has announced amendments to India’s Production Linked Incentive (PLI) Scheme for Textiles in a notification issued on 28 October 2026. Through the 2026 amendments, the Union Ministry of Textiles aims to address implementation-related challenges and provide greater flexibility to businesses seeking incentives for investments in man-made fibre (MMF) textiles and technical textiles.
It primarily introduces revised investment and turnover thresholds, differentiated incentive structures under two scheme categories, provisions allowing existing participants to migrate to the fourth application round (Round 4), and an extended implementation timeline. Round 4 of the registration and application window is now open on the official website between 1 November and 31 December 2026.
It should be noted that the detailed operational guidelines incorporating the 2026 amendments will be issued separately. These guidelines are expected to provide further clarity on the implementation of the revised provisions.
Establish Manufacturing Operations
We support foreign manufacturers with market assessment, site selection, PLI incentives, and investment structuring.
India PLI Scheme for textile: Revised investment and turnover threshold in Round 4
India’s 2026 amendment for textile PLI establishes two categories under the scheme, with different minimum investment and turnover requirements. Both thresholds must be met for a company to qualify for incentives.
Scheme Part I
Under Part I, eligible applicants must meet the following criteria:
- Invest at least INR 1.5 billion in plant and machinery, equipment, and civil works
- Exclude land and administrative building costs when calculating eligible investment
- Achieve a minimum turnover of INR 6 billion through the manufacture and sale of products covered under the notified MMF and technical textile categories
The incentive structure is as follows:
- Performance Year 1: Companies receive an incentive of 15 per cent on turnover, subject to achieving the prescribed minimum turnover
- Performance Years 2-5: PLI applicants/companies must achieve at least 10 per cent incremental turnover compared to the previous year’s turnover
- Declining incentive rate: The incentive rate decreases by one percentage point annually, starting at 14 per cent in Year 2 and reaching 11 per cent in Year 5
Scheme Part II
Part II provides a lower investment and turnover threshold, making the scheme accessible to applicants with comparatively smaller investment plans.
Eligible applicants must meet the following criteria:
- Invest at least INR 500 million in plant and machinery, equipment, and civil works
- Exclude land and administrative building costs from eligible investment
- Achieve a minimum turnover of INR 1 billion through the manufacture and sale of notified MMF and technical textile products
The incentive structure is as follows:
- Performance Year 1: Companies receive an incentive of 11 per cent on turnover, subject to achieving the prescribed minimum turnover
- Performance Years 2-5: PLI applicants/companies must achieve at least 10 per cent incremental turnover over compared to the previous year’s turnover
- Declining incentive rate: The incentive rate decreases by one percentage point annually, starting at 10 per cent in Year 2 and reaching 7 per cent in Year 5
Common condition
Under both categories, only sales transacted through normal banking channels will qualify for calculating eligible turnover and incentives.
Migration of existing textile PLI participants to Round 4
Amendments to the textile PLI scheme allow existing participating companies from Rounds 1, 2 and 3 to migrate to Round 4, subject to specific conditions.
Companies that have not claimed or received any incentives under their existing applications can opt for Round 4. However, they must withdraw their existing applications under the earlier rounds, as applicable, to become eligible for migration.
This provision gives existing participants an opportunity to participate under the revised investment and incentive framework rather than continue under their earlier application conditions.
Treatment of investments already made by migrating applicants
Recent changes also clarify how investments made before Round 4 will be considered when calculating eligible investment for companies migrating from earlier rounds.
The following provisions apply:
- Eligible investment period: Investments made between 24 September 2021 (the date the PLI Scheme was introduced) and 31 March 2026 will be considered at their actual cost.
- Condition for investment recognition: This treatment applies where the applicant has not commenced production or generated turnover from the investment.
- Depreciation adjustment: If production or turnover has already commenced, depreciation on the capitalised assets will be charged for the period from 1 April 2026 to 31 March 2027.
- Depreciation calculation: The depreciation rate will be determined in accordance with the Companies Act, 2013.
These provisions are specifically intended for applicants migrating from earlier rounds. They do not apply to new applicants applying directly under Round 4.
Extension of the textile PLI scheme implementation period
The amendment extends the PLI Scheme’s implementation timeline for Round 4 participants until FY 2033-34. FY 2032-33 will be the final performance year, while FY 2033-34 will be the final year for claiming incentives.
The revised implementation schedule provides two years of gestation before the commencement of the five performance years.
| Scheme period | Financial year | 
| Gestation Year 1 | FY 2026-27 | 
| Gestation Year 2 | FY 2027-28 | 
| Performance Year 1 | FY 2028-29 | 
| Performance Year 2 | FY 2029-30 | 
| Performance Year 3 | FY 2030-31 | 
| Performance Year 4 | FY 2031-32 | 
| Performance Year 5 | FY 2032-33 | 
| Final incentive claim year | FY 2033-34 | 
The corresponding incentive claims will be made in the financial year immediately following each performance year. For instance, incentives for FY 2028-29 will be claimed in FY 2029-30.
Evaluate PLI Incentives
Assess your eligibility for the Textile PLI Scheme, understand the revised investment and turnover criteria, and identify available incentives.
What the PLI scheme amendments mean for textile manufacturers and investors
Indi’s revised framework has several implications for businesses considering investments in India’s MMF and technical textile segments.
- Greater flexibility in investment planning: The introduction of two investment categories, with thresholds of INR 1.5 billion and INR 500 million, provides different entry points for businesses with varying investment capacities.
- Performance-linked incentive structure: Companies must meet both the minimum investment and turnover requirements. They must also demonstrate at least 10 per cent incremental turnover growth annually from Performance Year 2 onwards to qualify for subsequent incentives.
- Migration opportunities for existing participants: Companies that have not claimed or received incentives under earlier rounds can consider migrating to Round 4, subject to withdrawing their existing applications.
- Recognition of historical investments: Eligible investments made between 24 September 2021 and 31 March 2026 can be considered at actual cost for migrating applicants, subject to the conditions governing commencement of production or turnover and depreciation.
- Longer implementation and investment horizon: The two-year gestation period, followed by five performance years, gives participating businesses additional time to establish production capacity. It can also help companies achieve the prescribed turnover thresholds.
India PLI Scheme for textile: Progress & performance as of March 2026
As of 31 March 2026, the central government has approved 170 companies under the PLI scheme for textiles.

high_priority_articles.title: India moves to resolve Scotch tariff dispute, assures 75% duty on bulk imports: Report - The Times of India
high_priority_articles.summary: India moves to resolve Scotch tariff dispute, assures 75% duty on bulk imports: Report  The Times of India
high_priority_articles.full_text:
The government has moved to resolve a dispute over Scotch whisky imports under the UK trade pact, assuring liquor companies that bulk shipments qualify for the reduced 75 percent import duty after tax officials questioned their eligibility for the concession.
According to a Reuters report citing six people with direct knowledge of the matter, commerce ministry officials gave the assurance during a closed-door meeting with liquor industry executives on Monday, saying New Delhi would honour the trade agreement in letter and spirit.
One government source said, "We are potentially moving towards a resolution. Bulk Scotch whisky imports are indeed part of concessions under the trade deal."
A second source said commerce secretary Rajesh Agrawal told attendees that necessary steps were being taken to address the issue "so that the duty concession on bulk Scotch whisky is not impaired".
The dispute centres on the agreement to reduce import duty on Scotch whisky in India from 150 per cent to 75 percent under the India-UK Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA), which came into effect in July 2026. 
However, tax officials had told liquor companies that the reduced duty did not apply to Scotch imported in bulk containers.
The disagreement is significant because around 80 percent of Scotch whisky shipped to India arrives in bulk rather than in finished bottles.
These imports are used by Indian manufacturers to produce Indian-Made Foreign Liquor (IMFL) whisky by blending Scotch with other spirits and ingredients. The industry maintains that both bottled and bulk Scotch imports should qualify for the reduced tariff under the trade agreement.
The dispute has affected major liquor companies, including Diageo and Pernod Ricard, as well as Indian manufacturers Radico Khaitan and Allied Blenders and Distillers. Tax officials searched the offices of several companies in recent days and questioned executives over the classification and eligibility of bulk Scotch imports.
The issue has also drawn attention from Britain and Scotland. The British government said it was working with New Delhi to resolve the matter, while the Scottish government separately raised concerns over the treatment of bulk Scotch imports.
Scotch exports to India were valued at $335 million in 2024, and the Scotch Whisky Association has projected that the trade agreement could increase exports by an additional $1.34 billion over five years.

high_priority_articles.title: [India's H1 steel exports to EU fall ~20% YoY as EU quotas tighten and CBAM applies] - Shanghai Metals Market
high_priority_articles.summary: [India's H1 steel exports to EU fall ~20% YoY as EU quotas tighten and CBAM applies]  Shanghai Metals Market
high_priority_articles.full_text:
India's iron and steel exports to the EU fell 19.8% year on year in volume to 1.53 million tonnes in the first half of FY27 (April–September), from 1.91 million tonnes a year earlier, according to an analysis of commerce ministry data. Export value fell 17% to $1.48 billion. September shipments halved year on year to 197,433 tonnes (-50.4%), after 316,414 tonnes in July (-2.3%) and 387,143 tonnes in August, largely unchanged. Second-quarter shipments to the EU were about 901,000 tonnes, down 18.8% YoY, with September accounting for nearly 97% of the quarterly decline.
Over the same April–September period, exports to Africa rose 76.5% in value to $334.2 million, with volumes up 96%; exports to the Americas rose to $1.42 billion from $654.3 million (+117.1%), with volumes up 262%; exports to Europe as a whole (the EU, EFTA and other European countries) fell 4.1% in value to $2.11 billion, with volumes down 6%.
In background, the EU has applied a tighter steel import regime since July 1, cutting the annual duty-free import quota to 18.3 million tonnes from 33.8 million tonnes and raising the tariff on above-quota shipments to 50% from 25%. According to an analysis by the London School of Economics' Grantham Research Institute, India's country-specific quota was cut to 1.94 million tonnes from 2.79 million tonnes (about -30%), with hot-rolled sheet and strip quotas down 34% and cold-rolled sheet quotas down 59%. The EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) entered its definitive phase in January, with the first certificate surrender due in 2027. The report also noted that the trade data cannot establish whether India's product-specific quotas were exhausted in September, making it difficult to attribute the decline entirely to the restrictions. [SMM Iron Ore]

high_priority_articles.title: Fighting returns to Kherson region after longest Ukraine war ceasefire - BBC
high_priority_articles.summary: Fighting returns to Kherson region after longest Ukraine war ceasefire  BBCOperational update for the period from 06:00 on November 1 to 06:00 on November 2, 2026  Mezha.netRussian Forces Shell Kherson and Antonivka: Two Civilians Injured  most.ks.uaA brief ceasefire in Ukraine's Kherson region has ended  NPRIn Kherson, several men stepped on landmines—they were hospitalized  UA.NEWS
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Fighting has resumed in Ukraine's Kherson after a six-day truce brought quiet to the front-line region for the first time in years.
The ceasefire - the longest since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022 - allowed hundreds of people trapped in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky and its surroundings to be evacuated.
On Monday morning, local authorities confirmed that strikes had resumed, saying Moscow had hit a medical facility in Kherson city centre. They also said a 62-year-old woman and a 73-year-old man were injured when a Russian drone attacked the car they were travelling in.
Ukraine also accused Russian forces of using the humanitarian ceasefire to strengthen their military positions, rotate units and deliver ammunition.
"The enemy used the humanitarian pause to set up their positions," said Ukraine's General Staff, adding they had recorded rotation of Russian units, expansion of anti-drone equipment on the roads, and delivery of ammunition.
The Kremlin appeared to corroborate this when spokesman Dmitry Peskov said it was "reasonable to assume that the Ukrainian army also used this period for the necessary regrouping".
"It is a completely standard practice in such situations," he added.
The ceasefire had been brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump. Both Kyiv and Moscow thanked her repeatedly, though no details of her involvement were shared.
An unusual show of cooperation came from Russia's human rights ombudsman Yana Lantratova and her Ukrainian counterpart Dmytro Lubinets. The pair oversaw the ceasefire, travelled into Oleshky and were filmed speaking to residents together. They publicly thanked each other for their work, often highlighting that no violations of the ceasefire had been observed.
Both Lantratova and Lubinets called for the initiative to be repeated elsewhere, and Ukraine repeatedly said it would be prepared to observe similar ceasefires on a national level too.
But many have questioned whether this will lead to more cooperation and further truces.
In fact, the Kremlin swiftly dismissed the idea even as the ceasefire was under way, calling Oleshky "an isolated case" which would not affect the "settlement process" – a euphemism for the stalled peace talks. "There are no similar plans or initiatives," Peskov reiterated on Monday.
And although last week the guns fell silent in Kherson region, elsewhere in Ukraine Russia's air strikes continued, killing scores of civilians and destroying crucial infrastructure.
The decision to observe an unusually broad and comparatively lengthy ceasefire in and around Oleshky was therefore a notable exception.
The ceasefire's observance appears, at least in part, to have been linked to Melania Trump's reported involvement. By violating the truce, Moscow would have risked undermining its own efforts to cultivate the crucial relationship with her husband, US President Donald Trump.
Some commentators have argued that Trump himself would be interested in presenting the Oleshky ceasefire as a foreign policy achievement scored days before the US midterm elections on Tuesday.
"I totally get why our official representatives need to 'play along' with the US first lady on Oleshky," said Artyom Sheynin, a prominent figure on Russian state TV.
"I understand why it's so important to create a 'success story' ahead of the elections for the US president, whose wife 'achieved a ceasefire' in Oleshky."
Kyiv, too, had its reasons to be fully compliant. Although relations with the US and its president are often fraught, Ukraine continues to rely heavily on US intelligence and US-made Patriot air defence missiles to counter Russian aerial attacks. Ahead of another tough winter of war, continued American support is essential to protect Ukrainian skies from Russia's assaults.
But though the ceasefire may have been born out of political calculation rather than purely humanitarian compassion, it also resulted in hundreds of civilians escaping.
There were emotional scenes when hundreds of Oleshky residents arrived in northern Ukraine on Saturday. Many were met by tearful relatives they had not seen in years. To the journalists waiting, the evacuees told of years of hunger and hardship in a destroyed town.
The hundreds of residents who decided to stay behind will receive monthly humanitarian aid deliveries, Lantratova said, adding that decision too was the result of Melania Trump's mediation.
Yet the troop rotations and resupply efforts show that neither side is expecting Oleshky to be a blueprint for lasting respite in the future.
As Kherson came under fire again, Ukrainian drones hit several energy facilities across four Russian regions. In Samara, residents reported hearing explosions and seeing black plumes of smoke rising into the sky as an oil refinery was hit for the fifth time in a month.
If the truce brought a rare moment of relief to Oleshky, it has done little to alter the wider trajectory of a war that grinds on for now.

high_priority_articles.title: China's Stock Buyback and Shareholding Increase Relending Rate Cut to 1%; Third Batch of Swap Facility Operations Approved at Over 100 Billion Yuan - BigGo Finance
high_priority_articles.summary: China's Stock Buyback and Shareholding Increase Relending Rate Cut to 1%; Third Batch of Swap Facility Operations Approved at Over 100 Billion Yuan  BigGo Finance
high_priority_articles.full_text:
The People's Bank of China, together with the National Financial Regulatory Administration, the China Securities Regulatory Commission and other departments, held a symposium on the Securities, Fund and Insurance Company Swap Facility and a symposium on the Stock Buyback and Shareholding Increase Relending on November 2, to study and deploy the full use of the two structural monetary policy tools. The meetings confirmed that the Stock Buyback and Shareholding Increase Relending policy will shift from a temporary arrangement to a long-term institutional one, with the relending rate cut from 1.25% to 1%. The same day, a relevant official of the CSRC answered reporters' questions on stabilizing the market and expectations, disclosing a package of arrangements including optimization of market-support buyback rules, active ETF position building, and countercyclical adjustment of margin trading.
This is the third rate cut for the Stock Buyback and Shareholding Increase Relending tool since it was established in October 2024. The tool's initial rate was 1.75%, cut to 1.50% in May 2025, and further to 1.25% in early 2026; this round lowers it by another 0.25 percentage points to 1%. The meetings also proposed that financial institutions adhere to market-based pricing principles, reasonably add spreads on top of the relending rate and increase loan disbursements.
Looking at the tools' operation, as of the end of October this year, the swap facility had conducted two batches of operations, with 28 securities firms and fund managers participating, totaling 105 billion yuan (approximately $15.8 billion). Across the market, 902 listed companies had disclosed 1,110 buyback and shareholding increase loan announcements; including the shareholding increase loans applied for by the two state-owned capital operating companies China Reform Holdings and China Chengtong, the upper limit of applied loan quotas totaled approximately 440 billion yuan (approximately $66.2 billion), with cumulative disbursements exceeding 280 billion yuan (approximately $42.1 billion).
The CSRC official said that upon applications from relevant institutions, the CSRC, in consultation with the PBOC, has agreed to let 31 securities firms and fund managers conduct a third batch of swap facility operations, with requested quotas exceeding 100 billion yuan (approximately $15.0 billion), and operations will begin in the coming days. Compared with the more than 20 institutions in the first two batches, the participant base has expanded markedly this round.
On the buyback side, the CSRC plans four adjustments to market-support buyback rules: adding share prices falling below the IPO price ("breaking issue") as one of the conditions under which a market-support buyback may be conducted, and stipulating that market-support buybacks are not subject to the restriction that "the company's shares must have been listed for six months"; removing the restriction on declaring orders during the opening and closing call auction periods; requiring companies listed for less than 36 months whose share prices trigger market-support buyback conditions to strictly fulfill the share-price stabilization measures in their listing commitments; requiring companies with excess raised funds to implement buybacks promptly when conditions are triggered; and requiring listed companies to specify in their annual cash dividend plans a certain proportion of funds to be included in a special buyback fund, with excess raised funds included proportionally and earmarked for buyback cancellation, and gains from selling market-support buyback shares through centralized bidding also to be included in the fund.
CSRC data show that in the first 10 months of this year, 645 listed companies on the Shanghai and Shenzhen stock exchanges disclosed 700 share buyback plans totaling 237.7 billion yuan (approximately $35.8 billion), of which buyback-cancellation amounted to 115 billion yuan (approximately $17.3 billion), nearly 50%; 747 companies actually implemented buybacks worth 134.5 billion yuan (approximately $20.2 billion). The planned buyback amount, actual buyback amount, cancellation amount and its proportion all hit record highs. From 2024 through the first 10 months of 2026, the cumulative disclosed buyback plan amounts and actual implementation amounts on the two exchanges both rose 50% compared with 2021-2023.
Shenzhen-listed companies have taken the lead. BOE Technology (000725.SZ) announced on November 2 that its A-share buyback plan had been completed, with approximately 191 million shares repurchased for a total payment of about 1 billion yuan (approximately $150.5 million); all repurchased shares will be cancelled to reduce registered capital. CATL (300750.SZ) disclosed that as of October 31 it had repurchased 19.6059 million shares for a total transaction amount of 5.36 billion yuan (approximately $806.5 million); the current plan envisages using no less than 20 billion yuan (approximately $3.0 billion) and no more than 40 billion yuan (approximately $6.0 billion), with the repurchased shares likewise to be cancelled. Luxshare Precision (002475.SZ) had repurchased 17.6654 million shares for about 1 billion yuan. As of November 1, Shenzhen-listed companies had 231 buyback plans in progress, with an upper limit on buyback amounts of 118.2 billion yuan (approximately $17.8 billion).
The funding side is also gathering momentum. The first batch of 18 active ETFs began fundraising on October 23 and had raised more than 35 billion yuan (approximately $5.3 billion) in total as of November 2, with 16 products hitting the 2 billion yuan (approximately $300.9 million) per-product fundraising cap and closing, and three funds completing fundraising within one day. Nine managers including Morgan Fund, E Fund and Fullgoal Fund purchased their own products through proprietary or shareholder funds, with self-purchases totaling more than 2.7 billion yuan (approximately $406.2 million). The CSRC said it will guide the 18 active ETFs that have completed fundraising to accelerate position building, study the launch of multi-asset index funds such as constant stock-bond ratio products, and promote a floating management fee model based on performance benchmarks for newly established actively managed equity funds.
On margin trading, the CSRC will work with the stock exchanges to guide securities firms in comprehensively studying, optimizing and maintaining flexibility in risk-control metrics such as the margin deposit ratio, the conversion rate of securities eligible as margin collateral, and the maintenance guarantee ratio, moderately freeing up financing capacity on the premise that risks remain generally controllable. In January 2026, the Shanghai, Shenzhen and Beijing stock exchanges raised the margin deposit ratio from 80% to 100%.
| Key Data on the Two Tools | Scale | 
|---|---|
| First two batches of swap facility operations | 28 institutions, 105 billion yuan total | 
| Third batch of swap facility applications | 31 institutions, requested quotas over 100 billion yuan | 
| Upper limit of buyback and shareholding increase loan applications | About 440 billion yuan | 
| Cumulative disbursement of buyback and shareholding increase loans | Over 280 billion yuan | 
| Buyback plan amount in first 10 months | 700 plans, 237.7 billion yuan | 
| Actual buyback amount in first 10 months | 747 companies, 134.5 billion yuan | 
Note: Data sources are public disclosures by the People's Bank of China and the China Securities Regulatory Commission.
Against the market backdrop, China's A-share market has trended downward amid volatility since October this year, with the Shanghai Composite Index briefly falling below 3,600 points, and the unwinding of crowded trading structures in the tech sector triggering negative feedback in fund flows. In the first three quarters, A-share listed companies reported combined revenue of 56.74 trillion yuan, up 5.41% year on year, and net profit attributable to parent of 5.10 trillion yuan, up 7.77% year on year, with share price trends diverging from earnings trends. Over the past two years, the National Social Security Fund, basic pension funds, annuity funds and insurance funds have net purchased more than 1.5 trillion yuan of A-shares in total, and various institutional investors have recently been adding positions against the trend overall.
Dong Ximiao, chief economist at Zhaolian, said that shifting from a temporary arrangement to a long-term institutional one helps stabilize expectations across various entities and reduce the risk premium brought by policy uncertainty, driving buybacks and shareholding increases from emergency-driven to a normalized tool. Zeng Gang, dean of the Tianfu Liyan Institute of Finance, held that the rate cut lowers banks' funding costs, but the final financing price is still determined by banks adding market-based spreads on top of the 1% rate; policy can only provide a floor and cannot replace earnings improvement and corporate governance.
For the market, the highlight of this policy package lies in the tools' shift from emergency to institutionalized: the relending rate has fallen to a historic low, the institutions and quotas of the swap facility have expanded simultaneously, market-support buybacks are moving from an "option" toward a "mandatory answer," and active ETFs and optimized margin trading risk-control metrics provide support from both the funding supply and trading mechanism ends. In the short term, billion-yuan-level swap facility operations and over 35 billion yuan of active ETF position building will bring incremental funds; over the medium and long term, a higher buyback-cancellation ratio and the implementation of long-cycle assessments will affect listed companies' shareholder return mechanisms and institutional funds' allocation behavior.
